Mr. Speaker, the strike at Chapleau among some of the bush workers as far as my information goes has been organized through a branch of what is known as the Canadian Labour Defence League. I believe the locally active men are Minster, Vatchuk and Soula. I may be wrong about that, but that is my information. Efforts have been made from time to time by the Labour department under the Conciliation Act to get the employers and employees together, but we have found that where a strike is promoted under the auspices of the organization I have mentioned there has always been a studied attempt to keep the employers and employees apart, rendering impossible the application of the provisions of the Conciliation Act.
With respect to the strikers to whom the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette) has referred, I have no specific information, but I would point out that the administration of relief is entirely in the hands of the provincial authorities, and if they believe for any reason that satisfies them that these men should not under the existing circumstances be kept on relief at the expense of their fellow-taxpayers I do not propose to interfere with their judgment.

This salmon was pink canned salmon that had been found by the inspection board as unfit for food. subtopic: CONFISCATION OF CANNED FISH BEARING FALSE OR MISLEADING LABELS
speechtext:
I thank you, sir. This bill, apart from 'the ostensible reason for its introduction, really goes further and introduces some rather extraordinary powers. In introducing the bill the minister said that its purpose was merely to prevent the export of canned fish falsely labelled or marked, but the bill goes further than that. I will quote the old section, to which the minister takes objection:
Any can of fish or shellfish not labelled or marked in accordance with the provisions of this act or of the regulations-
These are the words to which the minister particularly objects:
*-before being offered or exposed for sale by retail.
Then the section goes on:
-shall be forfeited to His Majesty, and may be seized by any inspector, or by any customs, excise or police officer, or by any constable.
The words to which he objects are those limiting the interference to the period before the goods are offered or exposed for sale by retail. If that is the only purpose of the bill, why not simply strike out those words and let it go at that; so far as I am concerned that would be the end of it. In his remarks, however, and in the explanation given in the bill, the minister goes on to say:
Under this provision, even if cans are wrongly labelled, they cannot be interferred with until they are offered for sale in a retail way.
That is true under this particular section, but it is not true in a general way, as I will show later on; there are other sections that deal with that point. In addition, this bill goes further than the original act in two respects. In the first place it takes in any other offence, since it says:
-and not in accordance with the provisions of this act or of the regulations made thereunder-*

Meat and Canned Foods
That opens up a wide field; you might have a man punished under two sections, first under this section and then under some other section to which it refers more specifically. My second objection, and it is a very substantial one, is that this changes the act in a manner not hinted at and quite unnecessary. Under the old section, if the can did not comply with the act it might be seized by any inspector or any customs or police officer, and presumably the process of confiscation would have to be carried out before some court of competent jurisdiction. Now they have gone a great deal further; these cans are to be confiscated on sight by any inspector or any customs, excise or police officer, or by any constable. There is a great difference. In one case the police officer or inspector can seize it but he cannot confiscate it. Under the new section, which is sort of dragged in

I am sure the minister does not appreciate the meaning of it

the cans may be confiscated on view by any inspector.
What is meant by an inspector? According to the definition, an inspector is an inspector appointed under this act, or a police constable. That does not mean a civil servant; it may mean a political appointee, and the same thing in the case of a police constable. In British Columbia we have a very fine police system, but in some places police are appointed by political influence. Certainly in this instance the inspector is so appointed. Who is the inspector, anyhow, under the act? His duty is to deal with abattoirs for the most part, and that does not make him an expert in the labelling of canned salmon. The point I am trying to make is that it is improper to allow a political appointee to have the power, the enormous power, of confiscating and condemning on view, and on no say-so but his own, perhaps a thousand dollars worth of canned salmon. Hon. members know the type of man some political appointees are, and I say that is altogether too much power to put into their hands. That some such idea wyas in the minds of the people who drew up this bill is evident from the fact that they put the following words in the section:
Provided that persons aggrieved by any such confiscation may appeal by petition to the minister, who may remit the confiscation on such terms and conditions as he may prescribe.
Quite so. What does that mean? It means that a man who has had his stuff confiscated on view by this constable or inspector has the right of appeal to the minister, and he can look to the minister for help. Does the minister want that? Does he want to be made the final court of appeal in cases like that? In many cases it will be shown that the
seizures and confiscations by the local inspectors are so unjust that the minister will be compelled, in the exercise of his judgment, to remit the whole confiscation. What will be the result? There will be, immediately a political howl to say that he was acting under political influence, and that that was his sole reason for so acting. Does he wish to be put in that position? I am sure he does not. It might be quite wrong to say that he was influenced, but it would be said, nevertheless. That shows the drawers of the bill had the idea that they were demanding far too much when they stipulated that a man with no knowledge of law, or even of the subject under discussion, -could condemn and confiscate without appeal, except of a political character, to the minister.
Then there is one further point I wish to make, and it is this, that the penalties are far too severe. The penalty does not apply only to this section but applies to the whole act. In the act are forty-eight sections. It is complicated, and in connection with it there are fifteen pages of complicated regulations. Under any one of these sections, and perhaps for an offence of only a trivial character, a man might have his stuff confiscated. May I repeat that confiscation may result from a very, very trivial offence. For instance, if the article is not labelled properly, an offence would be committed. Suppose the wretched cannery man spells the word "Canada" without one of the letters "a". In that respect he would not be -complying with the act and would be liable, upon the activity of some maliciously inclined person who wished strictly to adhere to the regulations, to confiscation. Some hon. members may say that I have given a ridiculous example, and that such a thing would never happen. May I remind my hon. friends however that sometimes queer things do happen. I recall on one occasion being in court and seeing a man applying for naturalization. His application was thrown out, causing him much expense, and he was told to come back three months later. Why? Because the judge said that the affidavit had been sworn at such and such a place in "B.C.", and he did not know what "B.C." stood for. So far as he was concerned he said it might stand for "Before Christ," and for that reason he threw out the application. May I point out that the applicant had used a printed form in common use.
Turning again to the severity of the penalty, may I say that confiscation for what might turn out to be a petty offence is much too severe. The time of imposing a huge penalty for a minor offence has gone by and it never did work very successfully. We can remem-
Meat and Canned Foods

ber when they used to hang little children for stealing a loaf of bread, but that sort of punishment did not work, and was not just.
Coming nearer home may I say that I remember an instance in British Columbia

and perhaps the British Columbia members will recall it-which I might bring to the attention of the house. There is a practice in that province called pit lamping, and it was becoming a considerable nuisance. Legislation was passed stating that an offender would go to gaol for not less than a month nor more than six months for the first offence. The intention was to stamp out pit lamping in the real Turkish stjde. What happened? The local justices of the peace, magistrates and judges were not going to see a decent man sent to gaol for a trivial offence, and the result was that they accepted the most ridiculous defences rather than send offenders to gaol. The legislation did not work out as it was expected.
I may say that often the penalties are too severe in these small pieces of legislation. The minister has stated that this is a matter of no great importance. Had it been a big bill the leader of the opposition would have given it a hair combing and the legal men on both sides of the house would have spoken. I must say however that in these small pieces of legislation the officials run away with themselves, impose the most drastic penalties and it slips through the house -without being noticed.
One final objection I have is that this legislation is not needed at all. In the explanation it is stated that the legislation is necessary to prevent incorrect labelling, but they go on to say the following:
While section 19 of this act makes it illegal to place any false or misleading mark on a can of fish or shellfish, the only penalty involved is a fine; but in order to protect the industry it is necessary to prevent wrongly labelled goods being sold either in the local or foreign markets.
And so on. From this it would seem they want a penalty greater than a fine. But what is the fine? Let us turn to section 44 of the act, which is as follows;
Every person who violates any provision of this act, or of any regulation made by the governor in council or by the minister under the authority of this act in respect to which no penalty is hereinbefore provided, shall for every such offence, incur a penalty not exceeding five hundred' dollars.
So that from a violation of section 19 of the act he is liable to a fine of $500 and, may I say, $500 is a substantial fine for wrong marking. Five hundred dollars is a lot of

money. The maximum fine for common assault is $20. You could assault your mother-in-law and get away with a 820 fine, and you could assault her twenty-five times for the same money you would have to pay for the offence of putting a wrong label on your product. Or, conversely you could assault twenty-five mothers-in-law for the same price.
Then there is a penalty for contravention of section 37, which is as follows:
No article subject to inspection under this act shall he offered or sold for export or import, or exported or imported, under any name intended or calculated to deceive as to its true nature.
Then, it goes on along the same line. Turning to section 31 we find:
No person shall offer or expose or have in his possession for sale any article subject to inspection under this act unless all the requirements thereof respecting the said article have been complied with.
A breach of any of these sections is punishable by a fine of S500.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
subtopic: CONFISCATION OF CANNED FISH BEARING FALSE OR MISLEADING LABELS
speechtext: That does not apply to falsely labelled canned goods.

subtopic: CONFISCATION OF CANNED FISH BEARING FALSE OR MISLEADING LABELS
speechtext:
The section states:
No person shall offer or expose or have in his possession for sale any article subject to inspection under this act-
That applies to canned goods. Then the section concludes:
-unless all the requirements thereof respecting the said article have been complied with.
Now, under section 44 as I have stated an offender is liable to a fine of $500. The explanation in the act says that it is only a fine. Well, that is a careless explanation, and it is careless legislation. I shall show it is not only a fine. There is a liability to imprisonment, and I shall show how. True, section 44 provides for only a fine, and does not stipulate any imprisonment, but let me quote section 48:
Every penalty imposed by this act shall he recoverable with costs before any two justices of the peace or any magistrate having the powers of two justices of the peace under the provisions of the criminal code relating to summary convictions.
I shall not take time to turn up the section as the minister can do it for himself, but under section 739 of the criminal code, chapter 36 of the statutes of 1927, gaol is provided. It specifically says that in a case where the act provides a penalty of fine and no imprisonment, in the event of the fine not being paid, imprisonment can be imposed. So we have the complete picture. Under one of these other sections a man can be sentenced

Meat and Canned Foods
to pay a fine of $500 or go to gaol. I suggest that what should be done is to leave out entirely this confiscation business because they are already liable to a heavy fine and to gaol. Is not that enough?
Further, I object because it applies not only to the section which the minister was told it refers to but to the whole act and amendments. The matter is covered in other sections anyhow. I do not think that the act as drawn is drawn correctly or drawn in a necessary way. No one realizes better than I do the need for having strict regulations to prevent the false labelling of salmon. That is perfectly right and proper. But just because there is need for doing something desirable, there is no need for doing something that is unjust and unreasonable and imposing restrictions upon the industry generally. The cannery owners are having a hard time, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) said the other day, and while it is the duty of the government to see that the law is complied with, it is no part of its duty to impose unjust restrictions and penalties. It is all very well to say that these officers will use common sense in their judgments. We do not know whether they will or not, and we must protect the cannery man in the due exercise of his business. If the minister had allowed this bill to go to the committee it could have been amended along lines which he and his officers would have approved. My objections are reasonable and would have been paid attention to.
I come back again to what I said before. We are passing a law by which any politically appointed constable or inspector can condemn a whole lot of salmon just because of some trivial thing, and the owner has no redress except to apply to the minister, who would very soon get tired of exercising his judgment. It is not fair to the industry or to the minister. It would be all right to have it so that the constable could seize the salmon on sight and go before some court before which the minister and the accused would be entitled to appear. Even a spy in time of war is allowed a trial. This offender is not allowed any trial at all. The constable can confiscate on sight.

There is just one matter to which I desire to draw attention. It was complained by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) that we were going on with business that we had not indicated. I think the Securities Act which requires the intervention of the attorney-general before a seizure can be made strengthens my contention that we are taking steps entirely out of proportion to the importance of the matter, when we vest in outside officers the right to step into a man's premises and make a seizure of canned fish which may be incorrectly labelled through a mistake while in connection with much more serious offences we require the intervention of a minister of the crown in the person of the attorney-general of the province before any seizure can be made.

The feature of the amendment that I stress is that it takes the power, the excessive power, of confiscation out of the hands of the little constable or officer and vests it in a court. Is there anything wrong in that? After all it is only summary conviction by two justices of the peace or a magistrate having the power of two justices of the peace. I will never be convinced that it is not wrong to put an excessive penalty on an offence. We might as well go back to the days of the feudal system. Was it not King Henry who was bothered by some priest and said: Isn't there some good friend of mine who will rid me of this turbulent fellow? And they went out and murdered Becket or whoever it was. It is on record that in the old days when they got tired of a politician or a courtier, they would say casually: Take him out and behead him, and that was the end? Do we want to go back to that 74726-56 J
system? In Turkey there was a baker discovered giving short weight, he was put in his oven and baked. The caliph, or whatever you call him, boasted that this one act of severity stopped the giving of short weight bread by bakers. Is that the system we want in Canada? Surely not. Take another instance. If I go on the highway at night with my car on which I have only one light burning I may be stopped by a constable and given a summons and brought up in court, but the analogy would be that the constable could step up to me and say, " your car is confiscated." My car does not cost anything like as much as a thousand cases of salmon. The offence may be merely spelling Canada wrongly, or something equally trivial.

Item agreed to.
Hudson Bay railway and terminals-construction and betterments (including E. B. Jost at $2,250) revote $117,500-$550,000.
Will the minister give us a short account of the business done by the Hudson Bay terminals since the last estimates were passed?
Does my hon. friend mean the business done or the construction work carried on?
I should like to include the business that has been done at that port.

During the last year the 'work on the railway and at the port was completed to a large extent, though this item includes a certain amount of money for finishing up the work as far as we expect to go, .though that depends on the future business at the port. If certain lines of business show a great advance there will be other works in the future, necessarily, but at the moment I can say that with this vote the work will be largely completed.
But you look for a continuous development?

Yes, of course. The work done last year included dredging, a certain amount of filling and the finishing of certain works in regard to water supply and such things at the port. On the railway, unfortunately, each year subsidences have occurred, sink holes, as they are called, that have had to be filled in, but each year the number of sink holes has decreased, and it is rather hoped that with the work done this year the road may be able to go on an operating basis. This item is partly for construction.
In regard to the business done at the port I will give what I can from memory, and if

they wish my hon. friends can ask for other details. In 1931 the first boats went in; there were two. In 1932 ten ships arrived and took out cargoes of wheat; last year ten ships also arrived, and in addition there was one ship of the Hudson Bay Company, the Nascopie, making really eleven cargoes outward. As to cargoes inward, in 1931 two of the ships had small excess cargoes of coal which they wished to get rid of in order to make room for a return cargo of a larger amount of wheat, and we took some five hundred tons of coal off their hands. In the second year one cargo-not a very large one- of mixed freight came in, and last year one cargo came in and one cargo of mixed freight went out. All the outward cargoes, except one, have been wheat. In the second year some rolled oats and other grain products went out. Last year a cargo went out in which there were two hundred head of cattle. Perhaps it would be interesting to have some of the details concerning that cargo. There were nineteen and a half tons of honey, a small amount of egg powder, some hay for the cattle, and 150,000 board feet of lumber. That was on the steamship Brandon.
How much lumber?
150,000 board feet.

Can the minister say
where that lumber came from?
It came from the neighbourhood of Le Pas, although we have taken a good deal of lumber incidentally, for construction work, from British Columbia, when we required fir or cedar for building purposes.

Can the minister tell
the committee whether the rate on cattle shipped to Churchill is advantageous, when compared with the rate to the eastern Atlantic ports?

The operation was carried on under the direction of my department and I have not an accurate memory of just what the rate was, but I can get it and give it to the hon. member when my estimates come up.

As wheat was the chief
export from the port last year, can the minister tell us how many million bushels went out?

About two and a half
million bushels of wheat last year, and about the same the previous year.

minister tell us what it cost the government to fit up that ship?

I shall give particulars
of that when my estimates are under discussion. A special provision was made to test it out. I believe the same ship is expected to come back to the port this year, for the purpose of carrying cattle. However, I shall give accurate information when my estimates are under consideration.
Has there been-*

May I answer the hon.
member for Muskoka-Ontario? He asked concerning the prospects for the coming year. That is difficult to say, but naturally it is expected that more grain will be shipped from that port than has been shipped in the past. As I have said, about two and a half million bushels, in round figures, went out last year. This year it has been arranged, partly through the work of shippers, and partly through the work, I must say in justice, of the Saskatchewan government, to send considerable traffic through the port. The Saskatchewan government has been very active in attempting to work out traffic for the port. Already the Saskatchewan wheat board have chartered two wheat vessels. The Dalgleish people, who were the first people to send in a ship are sending one in early in the season; it may be the Pennyworth. But there is also another ship the Brandon, which went in last year and is chartered to go in early this year, as well.
In addition to that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce who arranged last year for the shipment of two hundred cattle has arranged that the Canadian Britisher shall go to Churchill upon the opening of navigation. On that vessel will be placed from one thousand to twelve hundred tons of general cargo and two hundred head of cattle for discharge at London. So the prospects are somewhat improved at the present time, and arrangements are in better shape than they have been heretofore. This year my department has not done anything towards chartering vessels for that port. In other years vessels were brought in to a great extent through the efforts of my department. But now, when the port is a going concern, so to speak, it does not appear to me to be the duty of the Department of Railways and
Canals to chapter vessels. That matter is being attended to by shipping agencies themselves and by the Saskatchewan government. Also, as I have mentioned, the Department of Trade and Commerce have arranged for one shipment.
In regard to insurance it may be of interest to mention that the insurance rates on cargoes have been coming down. Each year they have decreased a little. In 1931 they were two per cent; in 1932 one and a half per cent and in 1933 one and a quarter per cent.
How does that compare with other rates?
I would say it is about five times as high as the rate into Montreal.
How does that compare with the rates into Montreal years ago when the St. Lawrence route was in a condition far different from that of to-day?

I have no doubt the early rates into Montreal were just as high as rates into Churchill. I should like to give the freight rates, as well. In 1931 the freight rates out of Churchill for grain were 3s. 9d., whereas out of Montreal they were Is. 6d. That is a little over a third. The following year, 1932 the rate was 3s, and 3s. 3d: out of Churchill, and Is. 6d. out of Montreal. Last year the rate was 2s. 6d. to 2s. 9d. against Is. 3d. In other words in the year 1933 the rates at Montreal were down to about one-half of the rates at Churchill, but about three years ago they were about one-third.
What would the total difference be if you were computing the rate on grain?

I have not the figures before me, but some time ago I saw a statement, which I am now trying to locate, where rates were figured scientifically, and the figures showed that a ship going into Churchill, and allowing the usual time, and taking into account the shorter haul for grain, and the decrease in that rate as compared with the rate, we will say, from some of the Saskatchewan points right through to Montreal, that the ship could make a better return on its space or on its trips or voyages and that the rates taken, altogether, are lower.

By Churchill?

Yes. But the fact remains of course that the short period of navigation makes operations difficult.
It is closed for ten months in the year. What has been the average time of navigation from Churchill?
That is difficult to say. This is a subject which usually starts disputes in the house which I am not particularly looking for.
You love it.

However, I shall try to give the information. There is, roughly, a period of two months with at each end possibly a period of two weeks-and sometimes without doubt that will be extended. My engineer who is familiar with this subject, much more than I am, has said that the usual period is from August 8 to October 8. However at each end of that length of time there are usually a couple of weeks.
A couple of weeks of good gambling.
Yes, good gambling. Of course, during that period, for the time being at any rate, insurance rates will be higher.
The navigation period is practically three months?

I would not like to say it is three months at the present time although I remember when I made my first trip up there in 1931 I met a delightful old bishop who was and still is up there, Bishop Turquetil. He has canoed the whole north country, and told me he was convinced that the period would be extended to four months.
I think he is about right.
In some years there has been navigation for more than four months?

Yes, but it has to be remembered that the shippers, or ship owners, may not take very much chance. I believe it is still in a stage of experimentation, and some time will be required to know how long actually the season will be. So if my hon. friends opposite wish to state it is open for a longer period, I have no quarrel with them.
Does the government receive revenue from the grain stored in the government terminal at Churchill?
Yes; my engineer will look up the figures.
I understand the government is absorbing a portion of the insurance charges ?
No.
They were, I believe, at one time.
No. So far as I can remember-and I think I am right-we did not at any time absorb any of the insurance charges.
What are the possibilities for further freight reductions out of Churchill?

I think it all depends upon * the amount of traffic coming and going. The ships that have come into Churchill so far have come in light, except for two cargoes. Naturally if the ships can get two-way cargoes it will cut down the rates, and as my hon. friends from the west succeed in patronizing the route it will without a doubt cut down the rates. But so far, and I am not saying this in any critical spirit, it has been very difficult to get anybody to ship grain or other commodities through that port. It has been really a struggle. The first two ships received a cargo through my department. The second season we practically had to do the whole thing, and last season we also did a good deal. But this coming season the province of Saskatchewan, and I think I should say this in full justice to the province, is making a really strong effort to get cargoes and I have a statement here from which I quoted a moment or two ago from Mr. Merkley, Minister of Railways, Labour and Industries, who has been taking a very great interest in this route, in which he points out the difficulties that have had to be contended with in getting a boat chartered. In addition, hon. members of this house on both sides, from that section of the country, notably my hon. friend from Nelson (Mr. Stitt) in whose constituency the port of Churchill is, have been doing everything they can. I can assure the committee that, in spite of what is occasionally said in the press which is not too friendly to us, this department and the government has done everything it can to give the port and the road a fair deal.

Is the department at present carrying on negotiations with Lloyd's for a reduction in the insurance rates out of Churchill?

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay

Oh, my hon. friend was referring to insurance rates? Negotiations are going on continuously. I have already given figures showing the cutting down of the insurance rates. That is a matter that comes under the department of my colleague the Minister of Marine, which carries on all the negotiations in regard to insurance rates. It works in association with the Imperial Shipping Committee and has done much good work in bringing down insurance rates. May I in this connection, without speaking politically at all, but just as a matter of justice, say that the Hon. Howard Feguson has worked continuously to bring down the insurance rates at the request of both my department and that of my colleague the Minister of Marine. He has helped to accomplish what has been accomplished, and as the rate has been cut from 2 to H per cent, or nearly cut in two, I think it is only fair that credit should be given to those who have worked hard to bring that about. But I thought that my hon. friend was speaking of freight rates in the first place.
Mr. MclINTOSH: I was speaking of freight rates at first, but insurance rates subsequently.
My hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Gray) asked as to the revenue from the elevator. Last year the revenue from the elevator was 858,000.
What are the annual interest charges on the Hudson Bay railway and the port of Churchill?

I do not know that I can give the exact figures, but I have them pretty well in my head. The cost of the Churchill developments, including the money lost at Port Nelson, was in round figures 853,000,000. That figure includes the aids to navigation in strait and bay provided by the Department of Marine. My hon. friend, who comes of a race that is very good at figures, can easily see that at five per cent the interest charges would amount to something Like S2,500,000.

Exclusive of interest what
is the cost of operation at the moment?

The estimated operating
cost at Churchill this year is $95,000. That does not include the deficit on the railway, which last year amounted to $163,000. In our estimates this year we are only allowing $10,-
000 for the deficit on the railway. In other words, we are counting on a greater amount of traffic.

Is that just the operating
deficit?
Yes.

What are the maintenance
charges on the road?

This year our vote for
the road, including operating deficit and maintenance-part of it this year would really be capital-is a little over $414,000, nearly $415,000. That is for the road alone. We are hoping that next year, with the ballasting, ditching, filling and such like done, we shall not require as large an amount, because the operation then would be confined to ordinary repairs, wear and tear, and whatever else there might be under the head of an operating deficit.

I would ask the minister
to make a statement following the statement made by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Bowman) with reference to an editorial in a recent issue of the Free Press pointing out that a possible cause of high rates out of Churchill was the excessive cost of stevedoring and of supplies, and contending that as both these were furnished by the government they should have been furnished at reasonable rates, but the contractors were permitted to come in between and take a shaving on the service.

I am quite prepared to
deal with that because I saw the article myself, and in addition two members on this side of the house, the hon. member for Nelson and the horn member for Dauphin, drew it to my attention. If somebody has a copy of the editorial available I shall deal with it verbatim because it is full of errors.

That is the reason you are
going to deal with it.

Yes, naturally I do not
wish to have errors circulated in the west giving a wrong impression. Of course, I do not imply that the Free Press would think of such a thing as that.
The first point made was in regard to stevedoring, and I will deal with that first from memory, as I recollect the circumstances very well. The department has nothing to do with

Supply-Railways[DOT]-Hudson Bay
the stevedoring. It is true that the stevedoring was done by a gentleman from Montreal, Louis Wolfe, a very outstanding man in that type of work at the port of Montreal. His arangements were made, not with the government-but with the ships or the shipping agents, and we had no control and have no control whatsoever over his contract. Mr. Wolfe naturally could not afford, in view of the short season of navigation, to take a big staff up there, and so to facilitate things as much as possible, and yet to be fair to ourselves, whenever ships had to be loaded or unloaded we loaned him some of our labourers who are ordinarily employed at other works in the port of Churchill. For these men he paid us the wages that we were paying them, and in addition we charged him 35 per cent. That may seem a little heavy, but we had to bring these men into Churchill from different parts of the country, some from places far outside of Churchill, and pay their fare there and back, and we figured that 35 per cent was a legitimate charge, and very much less than the contractor would have had to pay for bringing the men in from different places himself. My engineer tells me that the 35 per cent was figured out by my officers to be the actual cost to us. That makes it even fairer. If the contractor has made a pretty good profit on the stevedoring, that is entirely a matter between him and the ships or the shipping agents who engaged him. We had no connection with him in any shape or form so far as his charges for the stevedoring were concerned. I assume he has the right to a just profit but as to whether or not that profit was excessive, I do not know. That is a matter for the shipping agents and those who are dealing with him to work out. An estimate of his profits was given to me but I shall not repeat the figures because I do not know if they are really correct. These figures do not show a very heavy profit. If they are correct, I think his profit was only fair considering the time he was there and it certainly would have no great effect on the freight rates. Any effect would be infinitesimal when spread over the number of ships which ihe handled. I think I have dealt sufficiently with the insurance rates. While these rates are higher than those charged at Montreal, we have been gradually getting them down and are still working to that end. Another statement is made regarding food supplies and this possibly has prompted hon. members opposite in their questioning. The article reads:

Regarding food supplies for the ships, these are all provided from the government supplies at Churchill.
That statement is absolutely incorrect because the ships bring in their own supplies. They do buy a little fresh food from the government but they pay for that on the same basis as they pay for labour, cost plus handling charges. Last year the total purchases for the eleven ships amounted to only $646. The engineer points out that there was no intermediary to get a rake-off, if I may use that term, a commission or anything of the sort on the handling of the food.
It is sold direct from the government to the ships?

Yes, by our staff up there. We have had to buy a considerable quantity of food for the different camps as a great number of men have been fed. We call for tenders which are put in by large companies who deal in a wholesale way and we get a very good rate. Another statement is to the effect that the business is done through a contractor who is well remunerated. I have dealt with that already and I repeat, that statement is incorrect. Without meaning to be anything but gentle with the Free Press, which is a great friend of mine, I say with all due respect that the statements made in this article are about as incorrect as they possibly could be. I believe the Free Press has been given some misinformation by someone who misread the report of Mr. Kydd, and incidentally I should like to know who has been so busy as to hand out this information. Up until the present I have not seen this report, so the Free Press has secured a scoop.
Is the minister in position to make a statement as to how far he has gone in the construction of the Mafeking cutoff?

A survey was made shortly after the elections and I think a report has been made but no construction has been started. In fact, I can say quite frankly that until the Hudson Bay railway does considerably more business than it has been doing, we cannot expect any great congestion and probably will not build this cutoff until some time in the future. As my hon. friend knows, this is to provide a short-cut to Churchill and at the moment there is not very much necessity for this.

lMr. BEAUBIEN: I gather fro-m the minister's remarks that we need not expect this cutoff for a few years.

I would not like to
prophesy so far ahead but it certainly should not be in expectation this year.
May I remind the minister that an election is expected in the near future. He is one of the ministers who is always very anxious to carry out his promises, probably more so than the rest and-
Order.

May I remind the minister that should we have an election this year or even next year he will have to get busy so that he can go back into the northern ridings of Manitoba and tell the people that he has done something with regard to the Mafeking cutoff. The promise made by the minister at Dauphin and that made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) at Brandon were both in very definite language and there could be no doubt as to what was meant. Should the minister go back to Dauphin and the Prime Minister go back to Brandon during the next elections this question will be asked and I am afraid they will be put in a very embarrassing position. I certainly would not like to see the Minister of Railways embarrassed in any way as he is one of the most genial members we have in this house.

For the benefit of the
hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Beaubien), I may say that the Minister of Railways will always be very welcome at Dauphin. He has always had a very warm welcome in the past and he need not worry about any promises he made during the last elections.

It will be warm.
An. hon. MEMBER It will be hot.

So far as Dauphin is
concerned, the present member, perhaps with the assistance of the Minister of Railways will do his best to look after the constituency.

May I inform the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Bowman) that the Minister of Railways is just as welcome in the riding of Provencher as he is in the riding of Dauphin. So far I have not seen him there. He was supposed to appear but he did not show up. The people have read a great deal about him; they have seen his picture in the papers and they would like to meet him personally. I do not say that he would not be welcome in Dauphin, I am simply saying that he may find himself in a difficult position. The promise was made that the Mafeking cutoff would be built as a means of curing unemployment, and I am reminding the minister of this in a kind and not a critical manner. That is the only reason why I brought up the matter.

I have no desire to enter into a dispute with regard to the Mafeking cutoff, as that matter has been brought up practically every year. I have been reminded by the hon. member that I made this promise and I have always told him that I did not.
I desire to thank my hon. friend for his invitation to visit his constituency and I shall make every effort to do so. For his consolation I may say that during the last elections I visited some ten or twelve constituencies in Manitoba, and we returned nearly ten or twelve members. I hope he will give me a good welcome when I come along to see him.	.
I hope the minister will carry out his plan and visit my constituency.
If I had carried out my plans during the last elections the hon. gentleman would not be here.
That is a reflection on the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) who came in his place.

I will let the Minister of Trade and Commerce take care of himself. I might tell the hon. gentleman that the only thing that saved him from a visit from me was a rain storm. He can thank the storm for interfering on his behalf.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce could not say that.

I understand the
minister has had some correspondence from the secretary of a comparatively new organization in the west known as the interprovincial traffic conference. Mr. Smith, the secretary, who at one time was associated with the Saskatchewan government, has been actively engaged in promoting the cause of the Hudson Bay railway. This organization held a meeting recently at Saskatoon, and I should like to quote from a letter addressed by the secretary to the minister. It reads:
For the specific purpose of developing export and import trade through Churchill in a businesslike way, the interprovincial trade and traffic conference, with representatives present from western cities, towns, wholesale and retail
Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay

merchants' associations, boards of trade, and the executive officers of the provincial wheat, live stock, egg and poultry pools, met at Saskatoon on January 12, and carefully reviewed the entire Hudson bay situation to earnestly ascertain what steps are necessary to enable the Hudson Bay railway to handle its proper share of the export traffic originating in, and the import traffic destined to, western Canada.
The object of this body is, I think, to cooperate with my hon. friend and to reciprocate in regard to his invitation to the west to try to make further use of this new outlet, they passed a number of resolutions. As this letter is dated only January 16, I was wondering whether the minister had had time yet to consider the matter.. The minister knows one shipment of oattle has gone out via Churchill even with the very poor loading facilities there. I understand there are no modern facilities for bringing coal in by the bay route. A little memorandum attached to the resolution indicates what an interminable time it took to unload coal from the Pennyworth. As regards Churchill coal handling facilities, the resolution reads:
That in order to secure fair and reasonable ocean rates on export grain it is essential that every effort be made to provide coal and all other westbound cargo for ships trading to Churchill.
The attached memorandum reads:
The conference is aware of the time consumed in discharging only 1,000 tons of coal from the Pennyworth last August-five and one-half working days, or less than 200 tons per day-and it is, therefore, obvious that no vessel owner would' quote reasonable ocean rates on coal unless assured of proper dispatch, which evidently is not obtainable at present.
It is, of course, also a fact that Churchill' is the only port in the world without proper coal handling facilities.
I was wondering what the chances were for some of those facilities being provided. Of course, we know Rome was not built in a day, but time is dragging along and it has taken about fifty years to obtain this northern outlet, so that everything in reason should be done to facilitate trade coming in and going out of it. Cattle yards and coal handling facilities are asked for in addition to a request, about which the minister may have heard something, for a storage warehouse to be established at The Pas. The reason given in that connection is that it is to facilitate trade via that route. What hope has my hon. friend held out or has he held out any to Mr. Smith, or can he hold out any hope to us that some of these very necessary facilities will be provided in the reasonably near future?
I am glad to say that I can hold out more than hope, because at least some of the things .that Mr. Smith suggests have already been done.
What are they?

I shall deal with them seriatim. I have his letter before me and have looked into it pretty thoroughly; I was already aware of some of the requirements.
As regards coal, the resolution which the hon. gentleman read covers that, and Mr. Smith, to put the matter briefly, suggests that we put in a completely up-to-date coal handling plant. To do that would cost about $300,000. At Churchill we have a coal handling plant, a locomotive crane type of machine, which cost us, in round figures, about $50,000. It is true it is not a particularly up-to-date method, but when one remembers that the only coal that has so far come in to Churchill was taken there by ourselves, this does not encourage one to think of spending $300,000 at this time and I cannot say that we are even considering it. I mentioned this in part a few moments ago: The first year when two ships came in there, one or other or both had some coal that the captain of the ship washed to get rid of because he wanted to have more room for outgoing wheat. To help him, wre took this coal, amounting to about 500 tons, off his hands. That was in 1931. No coal was taken off in 1932 and last year we again took about 1,100 tons of British coal, the reason being that it was a very high type and one of the two dredges which we had there we were shipping around into the St. Lawrence basin in order to transfer it to the Department of Marine. We have done this because we have no need for two dredges at Churchill at present. Those two shipments of 500 tons in 1931 and about 1,100 tons last year, or 1,600 tons in all, which would make perhaps one-third of a cargo, constitute nearly all the coal that has been unloaded at Churchill and we took it there ourselves. Naturally, my hon. friend who is usually reasonable must realize that we would not be justified on that basis, since we already have a coal handling plant there, in spending at the present time some $300,000 on an up-to-date plant.
Any ships coming in there now can be unloaded by the plant we have. It is true it does not unload as fast as a modem plant would do, but in going into the matter some time ago with my officers I found that the slowness of the unloading was due rather to the construction of the ships that come in there than to the plant itself. The keel of the ship has a shaft tunnel where the coal

sits upon it in such a way that the lower part of the coal has to be taken out by hand. It cannot be taken out by the clamshell type of coal handling plant and consequently it has to be shovelled into buckets, so that the slowness is largely due to the construction of the ships themselves and not to the plant. This may be of interest and it may be questioned by some of the people who wish to ship in coal; it may be questioned by Mr. Smith and some of his associates.
As I have already mentioned, we were told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that 200 head of cattle were handled out of Churchill and they were handled in the ordinary way. It is true we have not any pens at that port, but in this estimate we have a sum of $500 to construct pens there for 200 head. We also have pens at The Pas and Hudson Bay junction, so that we shall be in reasonably good shape to handle any cattle offered for shipment overseas.
Therefore I think, taking Mr. Smith's letter as a whole, we have already attended fairly well to his suggestions and I do not think the government, under present financial conditions, should be asked to move more rapidly than it has already done.

That is quite satisfactory as far as it goes. Of course I did not know what answer my hon. friend had made to Mr. Smith or what he was including in the estimates, but the results of the cattle shipments were so satisfactory last year, I understand they netted the producers $10 per head more than they would have got elsewhere. That is very substantial these days when the price of cattle is so low. And they anticipate shipping about 4,000 head by that route, so that would justify this new expenditure.
In regard to coal, we cannot expect much coal to come that way if there is such long delay in handling it. It is true there may be something faulty in the ship, but there would be no traffic at all if there were no port or railway, and if the facilities are lacking that would hinder too. This organization is very active in trying to promote traffic by that route, and of course there is always a certain disposition to make sport of a new route, especially one that is seeking to get some traffic that now goes by other routes. That is the experience of all new routes; they have to hustle for their traffic and against many handicaps.
May I mention another resolution that I have? It was addressed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, if he does not mind my mentioning it on this estimate, lest we
forget it on his. It is with respect to the interior terminal elevator at Saskatoon. I understand it is empty, and they are asking for certain storage conditions similar to what they get at Churchill, so that the wheat could be assembled at Saskatoon during the winter and be prepared to forward on to Churchill as soon as possible in the spring.
I will deal with that when my estimates are up.
The chances are we will forget it.
I am well acquainted with the point.
I mean I might forget it.

At any rate that is good news about the cattle yards, because with all the disabilities of any new route, if they are helped by proper facilities and proper pens it will be a great encouragement to ship cattle that way, in addition to the $10 extra they get.
Before I sit down might I inquire what the chances are with respect to the insurance rates? That after all is the bugbear there. I do not know the exact rates by the bay route, but they were represented by the minister himself last year as being four or five times higher on grain than by the St. Lawrence route, and the rates on the St. Lawrence are high compared with those for Atlantic ports to the south. So when you consider that these insurance rates are four or five times as high as on the St. Lawrence and the rates on the St. Lawrence higher again than the ports farther south, it is a marvel to me that anything goes out or comes in by the Churchill route at all. Something surely could be done, now that thei'e have been no more Bright Fans looking around for icebergs to nose into, as I think we have lived that down. There is at any rate always lots of deep water by the Hudson bay route; the straits are sixty to one hundred miles wide and not quite that deep, but there is no danger as regards depth of water. The same thing is true in entering Churchill; there is abundance of water even at low tide and abundance of shelter when you are in the harbour. There is no earthly reason that I can see why there should be such ghastly insurance rates by the bay route after at least two years of trial. I fear that until something is done in the way of the government

carrying part of that insurance or the establishing of a national marine insurance branch in the marine department, not for that port alone but for all the ports of Canada and doing it at cost, they will all suffer. I might take a few minutes to enlighten some hon. members on the situation at Churchill. Some question was raised about the length of the season. May I say that the season at present taken as being the navigation season is that set by the marine insurance underwriters at London, not the actual season prevailing at Churchill. The underwriters say a boat must pass out of the straits before October 15. There has only been one attempt on the part of this government to make any investigation into ice conditions in Hudson bay or straits. That tvas in 1927 and 1928, when the late government

1 give them credit for it-sent a fleet of airplanes there and established three bases in the straits, known as bases A, B and C. Instructions were given to fly the straits every day -that was fit for flying and gather data. I think we are justified in accepting their statements as being at least something towards an accurate representation of ice conditions in the straits, and from their observations I take the following particulars:

In spite of this our friends in the old country tell us that boats must be out of the straits on or before October 15. Many captains and other men who know those northern waters, men who are not making guesses-I name only one, Captain Bernier-do not hesitate to say that the season is much longer than the underwriters allow. The point I want to make is that no real investigation has ever been made in late fall and when anyone says that the navigation season at Churchill is from the 7th of August to the 15th of October he is simply using the dates set by the marine underwriters in England, who do not know much more about it than a lot of hon. gentlemen in this house.

An icebreaker could keep the port of Churchill open for perhaps two or three weeks longer than it is open to-day. That is being done in other parts of Canada; you only have to refer to the estimates to see how much is being spent for icebreakers on the St. Lawrence. I am not going into that, however. With regard to the insurance rates, the minister covered the situation with regard to the discrepancies between Churchill and Montreal. With regard to the advantages of Churchill, I may say that it is approximately the same distance from Churchill to Liverpool as it is from Halifax to Liverpool, and we all know the difficulties that ships experience in going down that long, tortuous St. Lawrence river. The Pennyworth was mentioned by the minister, who said there was some hope of her coming to Churchill next year. I want to disabuse his mind on that score. The Pennyworth, after making two trips to Churchill, piled up on the Isle of Orleans in the St. Lawrence and was a total loss. When in Churchill the captain made it clear to all that he would very much prefer to go (to Churchill than to Montreal. The last boat that carried cattle, the Brandon, made two trips, and the captain stated to me that he could easily make three trips to Churchill in a season, and intended to do so next year if he could get a cargo. That was the last boat out. The Brandon is owned by one of the largest shipping companies in Scotland, but that boat did not carry a penny of insurance on the hull. Yet the captain made two trips and said he hoped to make three trips next year; that is how much he is worrying about the terrors of Hudson bay.

May I ask how that shipment of cattle stood the journey?

They arrived in the old country in first class condition and were sold at the dock right off the boat. I do not think anyone in western Canada would be guillible enough to believe that the distress rates now existing in Montreal, which wrecked that route last summer by charging less than cost to carry grain, are going to remain in force. I notice also that the directors of the Saskatchewan pool have instructed the pool management to use the port of Churchill even if at times it is cheaper to ship via the great lakes, when freight rates on the lakes are very low, as they were in 1933, which condition the pool and other grain firms recognize as extraordinary and unusual. At present the pool, according to Mr. Gibson, one of the officials in Winnipeg, intends to ship at least 4,000,000 bushels through Churchill in 1934. They have 2,000,000 bushels stored at Churchill now. Mr. Brunswick, manager for Dreyfus in Winnipeg, is at present in New York trying to interest the Dreyfus office there in asking the government to build 2,000,000 bushels storage at Churchill, which they would lease for a long term. The Continental Grain Company are equally interested, and these are the two companies that shipped all the grain out of Churchill in the first two years of its existence. Only last year did the Saskatchewan pool become interested. I sincerely hope the pool will continue to use Churchill, because they represent the people who have been shouting for this route for the last fifty years, and if they are not willing to use it I do not know where else we are going to look for traffic. The facilities are there; they are the very best that money can buy. The port is admirably managed; everything possible is done for those who come there, and I am quite sure that this practice will continue. I hope that in the very near future the government will find it necessary to organize a proper port commission or appoint a manager there who will be given full charge of the port.
May I say in conclusion that in my opinion the best way to get the insurance rates lowered is to have the people interested in this route use it. A large volume of traffic and a low loss ratio will do more to bring down the rates than anything else on the face of 
the earth, and I sincerely hope all the western members will do their part in trying to interest their people in that route, because it means the economic salvation of western Canada.

I do not wish to delay
my own estimates, but I should like to say a word in reply to my hon. friend. He has been a very enthusiastic supporter of this route; in that I am glad to encourage him and to agree with him, but when he makes the statement that since 1927 or 1928 the government has made no investigation into ice conditions, I must disagree. As a matter of fact, investigations into ice conditions have been going on since 1926, and every year we are spending out of our estimates from $25,000 to $50,000 in connection with the investigation of ice conditions. I have asked my deputy and my engineer to give me some information as to how much the Department of Marine, which operates the N.B. McLean, a very fine icebreaking steamship, spends for the same purpose. They estimate that the Department of Marine spends probably $200,000 per year. So, if the figures for the Department of Marine and my department are correct, it would appear that since 1926 we have spent yearly something like $200,000 or $250,000 investigating ice conditions. I say that to my hon. friend because I wish him to have his information absolutely watertight, as apparently he had not before. I presume his reference was to-

I referred to late
fall and winter investigations.

My hon. friend is not correct there, because we make a late fall investigation. In fact, in a minute or two I will give him the actual dates when it was considered impossible for ships to go out. We spent from $25,000 to $50,000 upon the Ocean Eagle. The ship of the Marine department is the steamship N.B. McLean. Both ships conduct a very thorough investigation each year. They are endeavouring to get and have been successful in getting data which is of great use to the port. The hon. member was rather severe in his statement concerning my remarks a little while ago as to dates. I knew I would probably get into trouble, but I do not think it is wise to exaggerate in favour of Hudson bay. I certainly am only endeavouring to give the facts, and I suggest, not only to my hon. friend but to any other hon. member in any part of the house, that he will not do any service to Hudson bay, to the port of Churchill or to the Hudson bay route by making statements which are not in accord-

anoe with the facts. Of course, I am not attempting to suggest that my hon. friend did so intentionally, but I wish to point out that according to my officers we have had ships stuck in the ice and unable to get out on August 6. So when I gave the dates of August 8 and October 9, I was fair. I gave a date two days later than a date in one season when a ship was stuck in the ice.
One of the important points about the port of Churchill is that it does not matter whether it is Hudson strait, or the harbour itself which freezes up or gets blocked. If you can get through the channel of Hudson strait and cannot get into the harbour your ship is of no use to you. If you can get out of the harbour but cannot get through the strait, again your ship is of no use to you. Your success in navigation depends on the ice condition in both places.

An icebreaker could
handle the harbour, could it not?

To a certain extent, for a
few days. But when freezing begins it freezes up rapidly. I have read a number of reports coming down year after year, and I have learned that once it begins to freeze it freezes rapidly. No doubt it could be kept open a certain length of time if we were sure when the season would end. The dates given to me show that the harbour opens about June 15 and closes about October 20, but ice coming down from Fox channel and Hudson strait blocks the other end. The report of George Kydd, the engineer on the ground, states that in 1933 the following was the condition:	"On
October 22, the river is full of ice." Remember, that is on October 22. Then, on October 10, 1932, he said, "Ice down the river this morning." In 1931, it was October 31 before the ice blocked, and in 1930 it was October 20. I give those figures from the reports the engineer and the deputy have at hand. I had an opportunity to read from them when the hon. member for Nelson was speaking.
I have no desire to give anything but the facts. I do hope the hon. member will bear in mind that between the departments of Marine and Railways and Canals $200,000 to $250,000 is being spent each year in an endeavour to get data. In addition to that it must be remembered that ships are looking for cargoes, and particularly in these days when ships are selling for almost nothing. There is no doubt that men like Mr. Dalgleish, with whom I had the pleasure of crossing the ocean upon my recent trip, are only too anxious to get their ships in there
at the earliest possible moment. Mr. Dalgleish is a very fine old ship owner, a man who has handled ships all his life.
Information I have before me shows that last year the Pennyworth was the first ship in on August 13, and that the last ship departed on October 2. I believe that a conservative effort is being made-and I am not speaking politically-by this government, and a conservative effort was made by the late government, to give everything in the shape of a fair deal to the Churchill route. I believe all parts of the country may rest assured that, having in view the pressure from the western provinces, and particularly Manitoba and Saskatchewan, any government will endeavour to give a fair deal to that route. 'Certainly it is our desire, and I believe it was that of the late government to do likewise. The only point is that I think we should be given a little more credit probably, for what has been done. Certain people, perhaps for political reasons and perhaps for others-certainly not for political reasons in the case of my hon. friend

have belittled the efforts that have been made. I repeat we are making every effort to give the port a very fair deal, and with the improvement in world business, which we all hope has begun, I am sincerely hoping that next year Churchill will have a much greater amount of traffic than it had last year.

This is based on a communication I received from the Hudson Bay Junction board of trade and has to do with a matter brought before this committee this afternoon, namely the building of a warehouse at The Pas. The letter reads in part as follows:
A few weeks ago the Interprovincial Traffic Conference, meeting in Saskatoon, passed a resolution asking the Hudson Bay railway to build a warehouse at The Pas, Manitoba, for storing such goods as binder twine, wire fencing, et cetera, which would be imported by the bay route during the season and gradually sold throughout the balance of the year.
There are two reasons why the government should not expend money on the proposed warehouse at The Pas.
The first is that every pound of freight coming in by way of the bay to consumers on the prairies must pass through Hudson Bay Junction, which is ninety miles nearer the con-sunnner than is The Pas. I need not labour this point, as it will be perfectly obvious to you that the nearer to the consumer the goods can be hauled in carload lots, the shorter distance the consumer will have to pay local freight rates; consequently, the more money he can save. A single instance-taking all factors into consideration, a merchant at Yorkton buying barbed wire in less than carload lots would save eight cents per hundredweight if the distribution were made from Hudson Bay Junction instead of The Pas. In varying degrees, the same thing is true of all commodities.
The second reason is that there are already private companies interested in building such warehousing facilities in Hudson Bay Junction entirely at their own expense, and who are only deterred from doing so by the possibility that the government may be building in opposition to them at The Pas. Where wholesalers or others are prepared to make this expenditure, it would seem to be both unnecessary and inexcusable for the government to make it.
This letter is written by the secretary of the board of trade and is dated February 19, 1934. I have n-o desire to enter into any controversy between The Pas and Hudson Bay Junction in connection with the building of such a warehouse, nor do I wish to interfere in any way with the development of activities at The Pas, which is in the riding
[Mr Manion.] *
of the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Stitt), but I thought it would be wise to give the committee these facts in order that it may know any money spent at either place in the future may be spent wisely.

The railway is not likely to go into the storage warehouse business. At present there is a shed at Churchill measuring three hundred feet by one hundred and seventy-five feet and having a capacity of about 5,000 tons. Towards the end of the season this could be used for storage. At the present time no railway builds these storage warehouses.

I was rather surprised at what the minister said with regard to the bringing in of coal. He stated that coal brought in to Churchill could compete only within 300 miles of that port. I should like to know if he was referring to soft coal or to Welsh anthracite. This latter coal is used in Winnipeg and I cannot see why it could not be brought in 'through Hudson bay and sent down to Winnipeg just as cheaply as from Montreal.

I was referring to old country coal. The figures I gave were not my own but were those compiled by experts. They state that British coal will not compete with Canadian coal beyond 300 to 350 miles south of Churchill. I am informed that coal can be taken up the lakes and shipped to Winnipeg at a rate cheaper than that which would apply to shipments via Churchill. It is a startling fact when one realizes that Winnipeg is about a thousand miles south and east from Churchill. That means a long rail haul, whereas coal being landed at the head of the lakes has a rail haul of only about 425 miles. It can be moved more cheaply from Montreal than it can around by Churchill.

Practically all western cities are using American anthracite brought in through Fort William and the people on the prairies cannot understand why coal could not be brought in to Churchill just as cheaply as American coal can be brought in through Fort William.

American coal pays only about 17 cents per ton from the coal fields to the head of the lakes.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if my
colleague does not object, might I say with all deference to my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River that I do not subscribe to his point of view that the situation is such as to place the opposition in a predicament. The works at Big Chute were comprised in the contract for section No. 1 of the Severn division, and included the construction of a weir with head walls of sufficient height for a controlled navigation level above the weir of elevation 651.00. When the work on the contract for section No. 1 was virtually closed down in 1919, nothing had been done on the construction of the supply weir, and head walls, partly permanent and partly temporary with top elevation 651.25 formed the only control of the fluctuating level above the commission's power house. I protested two years ago, and I am protesting again against expenditures on this canal system. Before the capital expenditure is made I do hope the minister will make a careful investigation. If he can come back next session and tell us he has decided it was not necessary to make the expenditure, I shall be very happy.

As I understand the minister, the contractual obligations were undertaken in 1919 or thereabouts, and the work for which he is asking this amount is the construction of a weir and the raising of a head wall so as to control the head level. That condition has existed for the last eight or nine years-

Yes, from 1919, and I cannot see any great necessity for expending this money this year, especially under the conditions existing in Canada to-day and at a time when the government feels compelled to

reduce expenditures on undertakings of greater importance to the public in general than this undertaking would be. The minister has said that the canal system is a great tourist highway. He was not here
then.

do not remember the hon. gentleman making any particular objection to this expenditure.

Last year, for instance, we held up the expenditure on nearly $1,000,000 worth of estimates passed by this house, and I shall not hesitate to hold up the expenditure on this if the money is not required to be spent.

But I would point out that we are in a very different position to-day with regard to revenues from what we were a few years ago. Then we were not facing what will probably turn out to be a deficit of from $35,000,000 to $50,000,000 on current account. That makes a big difference, and that is why we should be all the more careful about spending money that we do not absolutely have to spend.
With regard to contractual obligations, as I understand it from the memorandum which the minister read, the obligation was not to the hydro, but the danger was on account of the inconvenience to boats of greater draft than could be accommodated if the water was run off over these head walls. That is different from a lawsuit for damages such as my hon. friend suggests might come from the hydro. My hon. friend has not the contract with him, but I would ask if he would be good enough to bring it down and lay it on the table or present it to the committee when his estimates are up again.
Very gladly.

In the meantime let the
item stand.

I have no particular objection because frankly I did not have as much information as I would wish t.o have.
Item stands.
Welland ship canal-construction and betterments, $250,000.

Why the enormous
difference in the expenditure this year as compared with last?

The chief reason is that
we have built the canal. I did not intend to give my hon. friend a short answer, but the answer in brief is that the canal is finished. This amount of $250,000 is largely for clean-

ing up purposes, to deal with contractors, for instance, who have claims and may get judgments, and so on. Most of this sum, half of it at all events, is for the purpose of levelling off slopes where there have been landslides, and for trimming up fag ends. The canal was opened two years ago, and the work is practically finished. I shall be glad to give any other information but I think that covers the ground pretty well.

Item agreed to.
Canals-improvements, $211,500.
Is this an annual vote?

Yes, a general vote for
improvements on the canals throughout the country. My hon. friend knows we have a very large number of canals, the Murray canal, the Carillon and Grenville canals, the Quebec canal, the Lachine canal, Ste. Anne's lock, the Soulanges canal, the Trent canal, the Welland ship canal-
And St. Peter's.
I forgot that.
And the Rideau.

None of this expenditure
is for the Rideau canal. It is for ordinary improvements.

Does it include repairs
as well as improvements?

I will read the details. It is for the replacement of structures which, in the course of years, have become unstable, obsolete or beyond repair; the replacement of equipment which is worn out; the enlargement or realignment of navigation channels, where such improvements are warranted; the substitution of more permanent construction on works where maintenance of the existing structures involves abnormal costs; general improvements that are necessary for the proper protection of canal property or that will give a reasonable return for the amount expended.

What proportion of this
is to be spent on the realignment and improvement of canal channels?
I should say almost none or very little at the present time.

Item agreed to.
Miscellaneous services-including salaries of experts employed temporarily, $33,500.

We dealt with this item
the other evening for about an hour and a half-

Supply-Canals-Elevators
Was there not an agreement that it should stand on account of the ten per cent cut?

It is in exactly the same
position as the item we were dealing with a little while ago. We discussed it very fully the other evening, when I gave all the details down to the last cent, which appear on Hansard, but because of the objection which my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) has just mentioned, and which was made the other evening, the item was held up. But as the item was discussed very fully the other evening, and as I think we should treat all these items uniformly, I trust hon. gentlemen will let it pass so that it will be in exactly the same position as the other items.

I think I was one of those who took part in the discussion of this principle last week. If we are going to vote any items concerning the outside services, I do not see why we should hold up any particular one. We are passing item after item with regard to wages and then we are attempting to hold up one particular item. Personally, I am inclined to allow this item to go through, especially as the government has placed itself on record as saying that there is a possibility that the ten per cent deduction will be restored. In view of that statement, I am ready to withdraw my opposition.
A question was raised the other day in connection with an engineer who was drawing $6,000 per year. I should like to know if he was subject to the ten per cent deduction.
He is not. He is hired by the month at a salary of $500 monthly, with an allowance of $800 for living expenses.
Are labourers who are hired temporarily, say for 35 cents an hour, subject to the deduction?

Yes. An exception was
made in the case of this engineer because we could not get him for any other figure. I explained the other evening that he was an outstanding engineer and we required one of that type for this work in connection with Beauharnois.

That may be true; on the other hand we may have an outstanding labourer, an outstanding electrician, or even an outstanding minister of railways, but in each case he would be subject to the ten per cent deduction. I do not see why we should differentiate between an engineer and
anyone else, regardless of what value his services may be considered to have. If I remember correctly, special legislation was passed to take care of judges and others in the employ of the government who could not be touched by the legislation in connection with the civil service in general.

I can assure my hon. friend that there was no discrimination. This gentleman was hired by the month; he is a temporary employee and this was the best arrangement we could make to get him. The man who had been employed previously was not considered capable of doing this work. We felt we had to have an exceptionally good engineer and we were able to get this gentleman. He stands very high in engineering circles and we thought we were doing pretty well to get him. That is the only answer I can make.

This vote would include $200,000 for the Trent canal?

If my hon. friend will remember, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) promised a reduction of $12,000,000 or $14,000,000. We all had to scrimp to do our share. Could the minister give the committee the number of persons employed in the government operated elevators?

We operate only the Port Colborne, Prescott and Churchill elevators.

mind.

This vote

There seems to be a
little difference of opinion on this side as to the reply made by the minister to the question I asked him regarding the expenditure of this amount. Was any part of this expenditure used for the Chicago exhibition?

parallel vote last year was spent in connection with the Chicago lair.

The minister said about
twenty-eight were employed. Are they employed all the time in judt this sort of work?

Yes, they are employed
at this sort of work all the time. There are some very able men among them who are artistic in the making up of exhibits, and when the exhibition is not actually on, their task is to keep the exhibits in good shape. Many of the artistic displays that they make or gather together and arrange are sent out for exhibition, or sometimes loaned-used in ways of that kind.
These employees of the department are part of the civil service of Canada, some in England and some here; is that correct?
Correct.

I remember seeing one of these exhibits in London. Is there cooperation between the department and various producers and manufacturers? Does Canada include in this exhibit the products of private individuals and industries?

Oh, yes. For instance in the Olympic show we took considerable space and then manufacturers would rent a portion of that space; but the arrangement of the exhibits, the gathering of them together and so forth, would be under the experts of the department. The exhibit is not made up simply of the flora and fauna and natural products of Canada, but includes manufactured products?
Yes, manufactured and natural products, very much so.
The minister said they rented certain space to manufacturers. Does that mean that there is a certain revenue under this item?

Item agreed to.
