What are the activities of the motion picture bureau that the hon. minister contemplates this year?

They carry on a very useful work, making films of industrial activi-

Supply-Trade and C ommerce
ties in Canada, as of the fish industry, lumbering and mining, or matters generally having to do with the natural resources of the country. Films are made also that are useful from the standpoint of attracting tourists. Of the industrial films, the automobile film that went out and commanded a great deal of attention is an example. These films, I might say, produce a certain amount of revenue. They are distributed chiefly in Europe but also in other parts of the world-some in Australia, South Africa and New Zealand. We think they do very excellent service in a general presentation of Canadian activities and resources.
I quite agree with that, I was asking if the minister had in mind any program for this year-whether any special industry was to be dealt with by these motion pictures?
There is nothing special in mind at the present time.
Are these pictures or films released to the general picture industry throughout the country and also in foreign countries?
Yes, to theatrical organizations as well as to private persons, groups, societies, educational institutions, and so on.

Is there any revenue
from it?

Yes, the revenue runs
about $26,000 or $27,000. Over a period of years, giving the round figures, the revenue has been $18,000, $26,000, $23,000, $29,000,
826,000	and $9,000. I have not the revenue for the present year.

I suppose, coming from the Department of Trade and Commerce, these are pretty much educational, along the line of showing the products of Canada, and are not used for immigration purposes. Is that correct?
The products of Canada and manufactured articles.
But not for immigration purposes?
No, not now. I imagine they were so used years ago, but not now.
Is the distribution trans-Canada in scope or is it confined to the larger centres of population?
A great deal is outside of Canada, of course, and it would be cross-Canada in scope with certain films. I could not say exactly what the distribution is in Canada, but it is pretty extensive.

And as between the
natural resources and manufacturing, are the films fairly equally divided?
I should say so. I should think perhaps the natural resources would predominate, but they are fairly equally divided.

The minister has told us about the revenue from this distribution. I would ask the minister whether the fact that a charge is made for these films perhaps limits the use to which they are put, and I would advance the suggestion that perhaps if there were no charge the distribution would be greater.

Our experience is the reverse. The department, over a great many years, has found that they are appreciated more if there is a small charge. The charge is not looked upon as a profit-making matter, but it is a fair remuneration. We expect a certain amount of expense, but the return helps pay the cost.

Do the trade commissioners in different countries make use of these films?
Mr. STEVEiNS:	Yes, they do, and frequently we have expressions of appreciation of the service.
Are all these films of a general character or do they sometimes have to do with one particular firm?

The object, of course, is to make it very general. I recall seing one film having to do with a large logging firm on the coast, and I could not discover what firm it was; it was typical of the industry.

Item agreed to.
The Precious Metals Marking Act, administration of, $4,912.
Would the minister explain this item?

This is merely the salary of the officer who administers this act. I am sorry to say that the officer, who had been in the service of the country for a great many years, died. A new man was appointed a short time ago; he starts at the minimum salary of that class, and that accounts for the decrease.

Supply-Trade-Publications
What are his duties?

The other day an amendment to this act went through, and at that time I think I described the act fully. This is a very important act, dealing with the manufacture and sale of goods made of precious metals such as gold, silver or platinum, including plated and filled goods, and so on. The act provides rigid and definite standards which, of course, are of the highest importance when dealing with precious metals. The duty of this officer is to administer that act. He watches with the most scrupulous care advertisements and so on, so as to minimize any attempted misrepresentation of goods, and I think his efforts have been successful. For instance, goods may be offered as sterling silver which are not sterling silver at all, or goods may be offered as plated silver when they are merely washed.

Or eighteen carat instead
of fourteen carat.
Yes, and the various carat weights of gold. AH this is carefully and meticulously watched by this officer to minimize the possibility of fraud.

Item agreed to.
Printing of parliamentary and departmental publications, $102,675.

This is the ordinary printing vote of the department. About $80,000 is for the bureau of statistics, for the printing of the ordinary documents of that branch, while the balance is for the publication of the regular periodicals of the department, such as the grain report, and so on.

Does this include the
annual reports of the departments?
It includes all such documents.

Has the minister * ever
considered whether there could not be some substantial scaling down in the printing of these reports? It strikes me in this way: we come here this session and we get a report for the year ending March 31, 1933, nearly a year late. It does not make any difference what government is in power; that always happens, and it seems to me there might be a great scaling down of those reports, because they cease to be useful for distribution, though of course they are useful as a matter of record. I notice one thing that is being done, and I do not know whether or not it has always been done; cards are sent around and members are asked whether or not they want certain 
reports. Does that mean that the reports are not printed unless requisitions come in, or is the report printed and supplied to those who ask for it?

We try our best, by the
card system and in other ways, to keep the number printed down to what may be required, and during the last year or two we have very carefully gone over these publications and kept them down to a minimum. I think we have eliminated all that we dare eliminate. I remember talking it over only a few weeks ago with the head of the bureau of statistics. We went over the matter carefully, and I do not think we could safely discard any documents that we are now printing.
With regard to the annual report to which my hon. friend referred, it does come late for the use of the house, but it is very highly valued in all parts of the world to which it is sent, as an official and representative document of the government. As a matter of record, and in an historical sense, of course it has the usual value which is attached to such documents. I do not think there are any other documents we could discard. Certainly I should be very glad to have the views of any hon. gentleman who might feel that some documents are unnecessary, so that we could examine them and come to a conclusion. Occasionally someone will say that a certain document seems to be useless, but upon inquiry it is found that there are many people who make constant use of it. The other day a gentleman in eastern Canada wrote me expressing indignation at what he considered to be a waste of money; a certain document he had got hold of seemed to him to be of no value. I looked it over and could not recognize any particular merit in it, but when I inquired I found that in a certain branch of industry several hundred people made constant use of it. It is difficult, therefore, to gauge the value of a document until one goes carefully into the matter with those who are handling it. I believe we have minimized useless and unnecessary printing, so far as we can possibly do so.

enumerate the publications to which he has just referred, and give us some general idea of the distribution?

Of course the expense of getting the material together must be very much greater. The minister was kind enough to say he would welcome any comments by which the expenditure on advertising could be cut down. These bulletins when they first came out were not unreasonable. I remember reading, for instance, that the export of whisky from Canada to Syria in one year amounted to nine dollars' worth, and it also gave the exports of women's hairnets to Palestine, or something like that. That may be useful to some people, but it is not very likely. The purpose of these bulletins, if they have any purpose at all, is to furnish appropriate and useful and accurate information that may be of assistance to importers and exporters. I do not think I am out of place when I say that those three qualifications are essential -that the information should be appropriate, useful and accurate. Let me give an illustration, one of two picked here and there, glancing over some of the bulletins, of what I think might be eliminated, to put it plainly. I read two sentences:
The quantity of goods and services exchanged times the prices of these goods and services constitutes one side of the familiar equation of exchange. In its original form the equation was as follows: MV=PT, where M denotes money and deposits and V the velocity or turnover of money and deposits, P represents prices and T the physical volume of business.
I do not know if the average business man gets much information out of that. Here is another example: It says that Three Rivers in Quebec and Sydney in Cape Breton at the 1931 census had a population under twenty years of age of 46 per cent, but not satisfied with that, it works it out fractionally, giving: the percentage for Three Rivers at 46-75 and. for Sydney at 46-33 of people under twenty-years of age. What use is it after they have arrived at the precise figure, unless' to incite a competition among other towns to try -to have more young people? Here is another example:
Millions of sausage wrappings sent to Germany from Canada.
Many millions of sausage skins, not the artificial variety but the old-fashioned sort, v-ent to Germany last month to make frankfurters. Occasionally the smart young Nazi calls them "hot dogs" when he treats his Schatz.

even when the wheat agreement is brought into operation? Are they going to pay us a higher price because of the quota we are to be permitted to place on those markets?

The answer is that they are paying a substantially higher price now because of the quality of our wheat. In regard to the wheat agreement, which we hope will work, it is not a simple matter, as anyone knows who has given it any thought. It is perhaps one of the most difficult things to be attempted in the way of international agreements with regard to trade, and there are many difficulties to be overcome. But the quota is fixed; it is conceived to be within the consumptive power of the importing countries, and we believe it is. Within the ambit of that consumptive power we get our quota of 200 million bushels, and I expect that we will get pretty well up to that figure. I am hoping there will be an adjustment in world conditions next year which probably will increase that. When we consider the export of wheat we must bear in mind that in the last eight years conditions in Europe have changed greatly. I believe one might say they have changed permanently; it looks that way. The fear of dependence upon external sources for supplies of food has had a tremendous influence on the people of Europe. I believe it is the condition we must admit is there, and probably will be maintained. On the other hand, if conditions in Europe do materially improve-and there are indications that they will-'there may be an enlargement of that market. These are things however which are entirely beyond our control.

May I ask the minister if there have been any special activities in regard to the selling of wheat in the orient, particularly China and Japan? I well remember the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce when in the session of 1931 he said we had a big potential market in the orient for the selling of wheat, and that to some extent it was taking the place of rice. Is there any activity in that section of the world?

Every possible effort has been made in that direction. There is one answer, however, and it is this: If the wheat can be sold to Europe under that fixed quota there is no harm done, even if exports to another section do not increase, provided the hole there is filled by someone else. What has happened in recent years, based on the information I have just given, is this: Australia has greatly increased its exports to China. Australia's wheat is more suitable for the 
Chinese market than ours is. The Chinese people want a wheat with a high gluten content. They use it chiefly for the pastry type of food which they call noodles, which is one of the main articles of diet made in that country from flour. The use of bread in northern China is increasing, but not to a very great extent. Then, a further consideration is that the Chinese people themselves produce a large quantity of wheat. Sometimes we get the idea that China does not produce wheat. Although it is not known precisely what they do produce, because they have no fixed system of statistics, it is roughly estimated that they produce about 600,000,000 bushels.
They are the fourth or fifth largest producers in the world.

Yes, and it is quite possible they may produce much more than that We do not know just how much is turned out; I have given the figure which is commonly used. The United States made a contract with China, on a credit basis, for the shipment of some of their western wheat. Their wheat grown in the states of California, Oregon and Washington is a soft wheat similar to that grown in Australia; it is not the hard Canadian variety. They do not export any hard wheat from the United States to China. They had a very serious surplus on the Pacific coast, and because of that they made one three-year and another five-year contract with China. They have not filled that contract, I may say. The demand has fallen off, and there has been an equalization in or a lessening of the spread between the depreciated currency of the far east and the American dollar, a factor which has stimulated the export of American wheat, but has materially checked the importation of wheat from other countries. That is the situation at the moment. We have done everything we can do to encourage the disposal of wheat in the orient. We have not however gone to the extent of giving our wheat away, as some people have suggested we should do. The reason we should not do that is, in my view this: The wheat flour business of China is controlled for all of northern China at Shanghai, by wonderfully efficient and comprehensive business organizations. There is no reason to believe that if Canada were to give 10,000,000 or 20,000,000 bushels of wheat to China for its so-called needy people in the interior, the wheat would ever reach them. We have gone into that matter very carefully, having been waited upon by kind hearted people who suggested something of the kind might be done. But there is no use in Canada's

Supply-Trade-Commercial Intelligence
giving 10,000,000 or 20,000,000 bushels of wheat to China if that wheat may fall into the hands of persons who, though not necessarily in need, would probably profit by it. Having carefully explored all these possibilities we do not know of anything we could do which would increase our sale of wheat to China. Of course we do a very nice business with Japan, and we are watching it very carefully.

Is it not a fact that the matter about which the minister has been speaking is really one of currency? He has mentioned the Australian wheat as being very acceptable to China, but if he will look over the record of five years ago he will find that we were selling far more wheat to China than either Australia or New Zealand. I believe the whole situation can be traced to the currency problem.

The wheat about which
the hon. member has been speaking was sold at a time when we had a great deal of cheap wheat. When we had a bad season with resulting tough and rusty wheat we used to send it to the orient, because that was one of the markets that would take it. Hon. members will find, if they check back, that when we had a lot of cheap wheat our exports to China increased.

In view of what the minister has just said, namely that China is usually in the market when wheat is cheap, may I say that in February last wheat hit a low mark, as low as it had been in the last forty years. Is the minister prepared to make a statement with regard to an offer which was made to this country by an organization which offered to finance 50,000,000 bushels of wheat into China. Is that true?
The hon. member has asked that question before.
But the minister did not answer it before.
My hon. friend asks it with a look in his eye which would seem to indicate there is something terrible about it.
Not at all.

I remember an individual waiting upon me. The reason I hesitated before, and still hesitate to some extent to make an answer, is that the precise details of the discussion are not very well fixed in my mind. The information I shall give is accurate, but it may be incomplete. A certain gentleman did wait upon me, and we discussed the situation, as I have discussed it with many people, and gladly, on many occasions. He did not disclose that he was representing any organization. I am not saying he was not, but certainly that fact was not left on record, or in my mind. As a matter of fact, what made the whole thing an impossibility was that the price of the wheat was to be twenty-nine cents per bushel. .
Was the grade stipulated?
No. 2 grade, at twenty-nine cents per bushel.
F.o.b. Vancouver?

No. There, again, I am speaking subject to correction, but my recollection is that it was a Winnipeg price. Yes, it was a Winnipeg price, because I remember in figuring it out in my mind I decided it was a figure we could not consider. That is substantially the story. In any case, the whole affair was incomplete; there was no definite offer made; and then, of course, there is the further point that we are not selling wheat. The pools and the dealers and the ordinary firms own, control and hold wheat, and can sell it at any time. Of course we invited these people to go to the wheat centre, at Winnipeg, and discuss it with pool authorities, and the exporters and owners of wheat in Canada.
To the minister's knowledge did they do that? Did they go to Winnipeg?
I am again uncertain. So far as I can recollect they went to Winnipeg, and the men in the grain business did not take them seriously. That is my recollection.
Is there a commercial intelligence officer in Washington?
There is Mr. Mahoney who looks after the commercial attache's office.
The Department of Trade and Commerce has no one there?
No.
And in New York?
Mr. Hudd has been there for some years.
And Tokyo and Paris?
In Tokyo Mr. Langley is the chief representative of this department, holding the title of commercial secretary; in Paris, Colonel Barrie.

Both under Trade and
Commerce?

Yes.

Supply-Trade-Commercial Intelligence
Are there commercial attaches at the legations in Tokyo and Paris?
In Tokyo, Colonel Langley is. Colonel Barrie is not known as a commercial attache, but he is always available to the department through Mr. Roy.
Both are in a different category from Mr. Mahoney at Washington, who is directly under External Affairs?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Langley is both.
Mr. Langley's office is in the legation in Toksm and he works in close cooperation with the minister.
But paid by Trade and Commerce?
Yes, and does all our work.

Canadian millers are often in a position to supply low-grade flour at a very low rate. Are our trade commissioners in a position to find out when there is a demand for this flour, and if so, do they keep the Canadian millers informed as to the possibilities?

We certainly keep ourselves advised and pass the information on to all our commissioners in all parts of the world.
I do not quite know what my hon. friend has in mind, but I would point out the export abroad of low-grade Canadian flour is of no great advantage to Canada except that it may get rid of a certain amount of material; but as a medium for advertising Canadian wheat and flour it is an injury rather than a help.
I say that frankly to my hon. friend because I remember distinctly an instance being brought to my attention some years ago where a lot of low-grade flour was shipped to the orient, and it certainly did the reputation for our flour considerable harm. So I should not think there is much advantage in the suggestion, except that in a year when there is a great deal of tough or frosted wheat, and when we are so short of higher grade wheat that we must mill a certain amount, then, of course, we have simply to do the best we can. Fortunately in not many years lately have we had that type of grain, so that the situation has not often arisen.

The question I had in mind has been partially answered by the minister's reference to the Commercial Intelligence Journal. I used to think that there should be some reference in the Commercial Intelligence Journal to the promotion of the sale of wheat abroad. I quite under-
stand now that it is probably more for the benefit of industries in this country, but I would ask the minister this question: Does-he through his department make particular efforts through the agency of the trade commissioners to popularize the use of Canadian wheat abroad for the making of better bread: and everything else that would go towards making people use more Canadian wheat, and: a better quality of Canadian wheat in order to get a higher standard of bread?
With reference to Canada carrying out its-part in connection with the world wheat agreement, I understand that a certain amount, of publicity or propaganda is now being used to promote the wheat agreement in western Canada. I would ask the minister whether or not money is being spent by his department or out of any of these appropriations in that kind of publicity in the prairie provinces-

I think I answered that a moment ago. We are not spending anything on that at the present time.
May I correct a statement I made a few moments ago when I said that Colonel Barrie was not known as a commercial attache. In his official description I find that he is described as a commercial attache. At the same time I can confirm what I said a moment ago, that he is under this department and his salary is paid out of this vote.
In regard to advertising Canadian wheat and pressing its sale abroad, we -have done a great deal in that direction. Shortly after I took office, and on several occasions since, I wrote personal letters to each of our trade commissioners supplementing what is ordinarily done through the department, pointing out to them the necessity of keeping to the very forefront at all times the marketing of our wheat and flour. I did that, not that I wished to disregard other commodities, but rather because it was an item of such supreme importance to Canada that I felt I was justified in doing it. Then in Winnipeg, in a laboratory attached to and under -the Board of Grain Commissioners, we had a chemist make a series of scientific tests of our wheat and flour, ascertaining the baking qualities, and so forth. He made a series of comparisons showing that a certain percentage of Canadian flour mixed with flour made from, we will say, French wheat, Italian wheat, English wheat, and wheat of other countries in certain proportions, would give certain results. The scientific data was all set forth and photographs were made of the bread baked at these tests. The whole -thing was set out in a very attractive little brochure which was

Supply-Trade-Commercial Intelligence
sent to every trade commissioner, and they were specially instructed in the technique of this subject, and also specially instructed that they must give every possible attention to the utilization of the information contained in the brochure for the purpose of encouraging the use of our wheat and flour. I merely mention these things to show that in these ways and otherwise we are doing the utmost we can in that direction.
The minister is satisfied that that scientific information has been put out to the people?
Oh, yes.

I should like to point
out to the minister, who is chairman of the mass buying committee, that a certain anomaly exists in our internal and external trade in regard to flour. In our section of the country, when we buy flour from. Winnipeg or the west, we have to pay more for it than people in Montreal, Halifax and Vancouver have to pay; and if my information is correct, people on the European continent, in London, Liverpool, and at Havre in France, can buy our flour more cheaply than we can buy it. Surely that is an anomaly that should be remedied; the Canadian consumer should not be penalized for buying Canadian flour. I thought it well to bring this matter to the attention of the minister, who is chairman of the committee investigating certain matters pertaining to our commerce, with a view to seeing whether we can avoid being penalized by having to pay a higher price than people abroad for our own Canadian production.

We have already made
a partial study of that question and the material we have accumulated has been passed on to the committee.

I want to follow up the
question I asked of the minister a few minutes ago with regard to the relationship between the department and the gentlemen in the capitals where we have legations. I am speaking particularly of Washington. I take it from what the minister says that Mr. Mahoney is under External Affairs altogether.
Right.

What I am anxious to see done, and I am sure the government is too, is that there shall be gathered together in one department all the information with regard to external trade, and particularly with regard to what is happening from time to time now in the United States, especially
with regard to codes and tariffs. I make no complaint, because I was treated with the greatest courtesy, both by the minister and by Mr. Mahoney when I was in Washington. They put themselves out and gave me the fullest information and have kept me informed since that time. From my experience during the past few days I feel that I ought to be able to go to some department to find out the latest developments in connection with the different codes which might affect Canadian trade, as well as the latest information with regard to legislation and tariffs. The Minister of Trade and Commerce may get this information direct from Mr. Mahoney; I do not know. H he does, it would prove of great benefit to me as I would know where I could get it.
No doubt the Prime Minister, as Minister of External Affairs, and probably the Minister of Trade and Commerce, know that quite recently legislation was introduced into the American congress to provide for an embargo on all fish products into the United States. This is of particular concern to those engaged in the fishing industry. The departmental officials gave me the best information they could, but there does not seem to be any place where such information is concentrated. If I may say so, I think it ought to be concentrated in the Department of Trade and Commerce. Let me give one instance. The lobster code has recently been prepared. In that code is contained provisions with regard to measurement which may seriously affect our industry, although we do not think so. If that information were immediately available in the Department of Trade and Commerce it would prove to be of great assistance. In connection with tariffs, there is a possibility of the application of section 3 (e), I think it is, of the American act, whereby if it is found that importations are taking place under such conditions or in such quantities as to prejudice the commodities dealt with by the code, action may be taken by the president. Information as to wrhat action may be taken or may be threatened to be taken under this section should be easily available to those interested in these industries.

We are supplied constantly with ail this information by Mr, Mahoney and we keep a close check on all legislation, moves, and so on passed or made in the United States, as well as in other countries. All this information is available at any time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The difficulty has been
that in countries where legations have been set up the governments will deal only through

the legations and not through the trade commissioners. Since I have held office difficulty has arisen as to the status of our trade commissioner in Paris. He found it difficult to approach the government about any matter concerning trade except through the legation. I do not know whether there is any international rule governing this, but that is the fact. The rule here is that information as it comes into the Department of External Affairs is sent to the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Agriculture, or whatever department may be affected. We cannot ask foreign governments to depart from their settled rules of procedure; we have to follow the rules they prescribe.
I was not thinking of an endeavour to influence governments; I was speaking more along the line of having news and information made available.
We have it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As it comes here it is
always available.
Has the minister received any information during the last two or three days with regard to this legislation putting an embargo on fish?

It is very difficult for me to express any views on that subject. All I can say is that it is being watched with care and everything consistent with neighbourly relations is being done to protect Canadian interests.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No item in any code
promulgated thus far by the United States has imposed any restriction upon Canadian trade.

I am not talking about
codes that have been promulgated.	*

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am just stating that.
The discussions which take place between Ottawa and Washington cannot be considered in this house until finality is reached. To do so would violate a fundamental principle of relations between outlying representatives of the government and the government. Once more I repeat, it is a matter of singular satisfaction that not one single item in any code promulgated thus far has imposed restrictions upon Canadian trade. In connection with the trade in alcoholic liquors, we had practically a monopoly as our commodities complied with the regulations while the commodities of other countries did not.

Every code promulgated
so far has preserved carefully the provisions of section 3 (e) which states that if goods 
are imported under such conditions or in such quantities as injuriously to affect the producers under that code, application may be made to the president to prohibit importations or to provide for licensing restrictions. While the Prime Minister is quite right, there is always the sword of Damocles held over our head. I was not referring to codes but rather to news as to the progress of information.

We could have news
about it.
If it is understood that we are to be given an opportunity to discuss the wheat question when the Canada Girain Act is under consideration, I shall have nothing more to say to-night.

It would come more
properly under that bill.
